raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart failure syndrome presenting toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, after exclusion of alternative causes. Early definitions emphasized onset in the final month of pregnancy through 5 months postpartum [1], with echocardiographic criteria—usually left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45%—added to improve diagnostic specificity [2]. Contemporary statements use a broader peripartum window because strict temporal cutoffs may miss clinically similar disease [3-5]. PPCM is uncommon but clinically important because it affects young women, may present with cardiogenic shock, thromboembolism, arrhythmias, or death, and has highly variable recovery [6-9].

Epidemiology varies strikingly by geography, ancestry, ascertainment, and access to echocardiography. U.S. administrative studies show rising recognition over time and substantial racial disparities [10-13]. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, especially pre-eclampsia, are among the most reproducible risk factors; multiple gestation, advanced maternal age, African ancestry, obesity, and lower socioeconomic status also contribute [9,14]. The overlap with pre-eclampsia is biologically plausible because late pregnancy is an anti-angiogenic state, accentuated by placental soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1) and other vascular stressors [14,15].

Pathogenesis is now viewed as a “susceptible myocardium plus peripartum stress” model. Experimental work implicates oxidative stress, cathepsin-D cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa anti-angiogenic fragment, endothelial injury, impaired myocardial angiogenesis, and inflammatory activation [15-17]. Genetic susceptibility is increasingly recognized: truncating variants in dilated-cardiomyopathy genes, particularly TTN, occur in a meaningful minority of patients and are associated with a DCM-like substrate and potentially less complete recovery [18]. Thus, PPCM is not a single disease but a syndrome arising from convergent hormonal, vascular, inflammatory, and genetic mechanisms.

Clinically, PPCM often mimics normal late pregnancy or puerperium—dyspnea, edema, fatigue, cough, and orthopnea—so delayed diagnosis is common. Evaluation should include ECG, natriuretic peptide testing, chest imaging when appropriate, and urgent transthoracic echocardiography to document LVEF, ventricular dimensions, right ventricular function, valvular regurgitation, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus [5,8,9]. Low baseline LVEF and greater LV dilatation predict persistent dysfunction; the IPAC study showed that severe initial LV impairment and Black race were associated with lower recovery rates at 12 months [19,20]. Large registries confirm regional differences in mortality and recovery: EORP and PEACE highlight that outcomes depend not only on biology but also on timing of diagnosis, background risk, and availability of contemporary heart-failure care [21-24].

Management requires multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric care. During pregnancy, fetal-safe therapies include loop diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers when tolerated, hydralazine–nitrate combinations for afterload reduction, digoxin in selected cases, and anticoagulation when LVEF is severely reduced or thrombus is present; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNIs, mineralocorticoid antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors are generally deferred until after delivery [4,5,8]. Postpartum, guideline-directed heart-failure therapy should be rapidly optimized, with attention to breastfeeding compatibility and shared decision-making. Severe presentations may require inotropes, vasodilators, mechanical circulatory support, or transplantation referral.

Bromocriptine, by suppressing prolactin release, is the principal disease-targeted therapy studied. A small randomized proof-of-concept trial suggested improved recovery with bromocriptine added to standard therapy [25], while a later multicenter randomized study found excellent overall recovery but did not prove superiority of a longer over a shorter bromocriptine regimen [26]. Because bromocriptine may increase thrombotic risk and suppresses lactation, it is usually considered selectively—particularly in severe PPCM—alongside anticoagulation and informed counseling [5,26].

Follow-up echocardiography is essential because recovery can continue beyond 6 months, yet relapse or late deterioration may occur. Subsequent pregnancy is a central counseling issue: risk is highest when LV dysfunction persists, but recurrence can occur even after apparent recovery [27,28]. Women should receive preconception assessment, contraception counseling, medication review, and discussion of maternal and fetal risk. Overall, modern PPCM care has shifted from passive observation to early diagnosis, risk stratification, genetic awareness, registry-informed prognosis, and individualized heart-failure and reproductive planning [29,30].
